meta.title: Twelve Grips, One Chord
meta.summary: All twelve C major grips in one table, the four ladders that show how each set's inversions climb the neck, and the rule for finding the third in any of them.

spans.text: Four sets, three inversions each, twelve grips — and it's one chord the entire time. Laid next to each other, the maps for strings 1-2-3, 2-3-4, 3-4-5 and 4-5-6 cover every close C major triad the guitar can hold, from the nut past fret 12.

Each cell is one grip; you've met all twelve by now. What the table can't show is how the three inversions on a single set connect — where the climb starts and where it turns over. The four diagrams below draw that, one set at a time, with no play button, same as before.
Strings 1-2-3 start their cycle at the nut on second inversion, climb through root position and first inversion, and repeat an octave up.

props.caption: C major's three inversions on strings 1-2-3, climbing the whole neck.

spans.text: Strings 2-3-4 start on first inversion instead, down at the nut, then second inversion, then root position further up.

props.caption: C major's three inversions on strings 2-3-4, climbing the whole neck.

spans.text: Strings 3-4-5 start on root position — the plain shape at the bottom of the open C chord — then first inversion, then second.

props.caption: C major's three inversions on strings 3-4-5, climbing the whole neck.

spans.text: Strings 4-5-6 start on second inversion too, low at frets 2 and 3, then root position, then first inversion up at fret 10.

props.caption: C major's three inversions on strings 4-5-6, climbing the whole neck.

spans.text: Strings 1-2-3 starts on second, strings 2-3-4 on first, strings 3-4-5 on root, strings 4-5-6 on second again — so "second, root, first" isn't a sequence to carry from one set to the next. Each set has to be read fresh.
Pick almost any few frets and look across all four diagrams: there's a C major triad on some set within reach of it. The chord is never far away, wherever your hand happens to be.
Finding the third, wherever you are
One more thing is true across every grip on every set, and it's worth being able to point at without hunting: where the third sits depends only on the inversion, never on the set.
Look back at the four diagrams and find the third in a labeled band from each one — middle, lowest, highest, cycling with the inversion and never with the set.
